subject: stats
title: Statistical Data
objectives: Distinguish primary from secondary data, and internal from external sources.
Describe the methods of collecting primary data, with their advantages and disadvantages.
State the components and qualities of a good questionnaire.
Explain probability and non-probability sampling techniques.
study:
Statistical data must meet five quality criteria: Relevant to the problem being investigated, Accurate and free from collection errors, Adequate in quantity, Timely enough to still apply, and Homogeneous — collected under uniform conditions. By nature, data is Qualitative (Categorical) — describing attributes like gender or job title — or Quantitative (Numerical) — expressing quantities, itself split into Discrete data (specific countable values, e.g. number of employees) and Continuous data (any value in a range, e.g. weight).

Key termPrimary data — first-hand, original, unprocessed information collected directly by an investigator for a specific purpose (e.g. a national census). Secondary data — second-hand information already collected and processed by someone else (e.g. figures from a firm's published records). Primary data is generally more reliable, since it hasn't been filtered or altered by anyone else first.

Sources are also described by origin: internal sources (an organisation's own reports and records, e.g. its profit-and-loss account) versus external sources (data obtained from outside the organisation), and by purpose: statistical sources (collected for an official purpose, e.g. a census) versus non-statistical sources (private or administrative purposes).

Seven methods exist for collecting primary data, each with distinct trade-offs. The Direct Personal Interview gives accurate, first-hand information and flexibility, but is expensive, slow and open to interviewer bias. The Indirect Oral Interview questions third parties in touch with the informants — wider coverage, but risks fake or non-comparable responses. Using Correspondents (trained local agents) is economical and fast but suffers a lack of conformity and unreliable data. The Telephone Interview is fast and covers wide geography, but excludes anyone without a phone and loses all visual feedback. The Mailed Questionnaire is cheap, wide-reaching and free of interviewer bias, with anonymity encouraging honesty — but response rates are low (often 10–30%) and it unsuits illiterate respondents. The Observation Method records actual behaviour rather than what people say, either structured/systematic, unstructured, or participant (the researcher joins the group being studied) — but the observer's presence can itself influence behaviour. The Experimental Method holds other variables constant while manipulating one, to observe its effect on a response variable.

Exam tipLearn each data-collection method's single defining advantage and disadvantage as a pair — CIPM questions often present a scenario and ask which method it describes or which weakness applies to it.

A good questionnaire has three parts: an Introduction explaining the research purpose, a Personal Data section, and the Actual Questions targeting the research problem — and should be clear, unambiguous, logically sequenced, and free of leading or embarrassing questions.

Sampling is selecting a required number of items from a population (the entire set a researcher wants to study). Probability sampling gives every unit a known, non-zero chance of selection: Simple Random (equal chance for all), Stratified (population split into strata, then randomly sampled within each), Systematic (first unit random, then fixed intervals), Cluster (whole clusters randomly selected), and Multistage (sampling in successive stages). Non-probability sampling is not chance-based: Quota (fills an arbitrary quota per segment), Haphazard (interviewer convenience), Judgement (researcher's own judgement of representativeness), and Convenience (whichever units are easiest to reach).
recap:
• Data quality: Relevant, Accurate, Adequate, Timely, Homogeneous.
  • Qualitative (categorical) vs Quantitative (discrete or continuous) data.
  • Primary (first-hand, more reliable) vs Secondary (already processed) data; internal vs external sources.
  • 7 primary data methods: Direct Personal Interview, Indirect Oral Interview, Correspondents, Telephone Interview, Mailed Questionnaire, Observation, Experimental.
  • Questionnaire has 3 parts: Introduction, Personal Data, Actual Questions.
  • Probability sampling: Simple Random, Stratified, Systematic, Cluster, Multistage.
  • Non-probability sampling: Quota, Haphazard, Judgement, Convenience.

quiz.q: Data expressed in categories such as Yes/No, True/False or Success/Failure is called …… data.
quiz.why: Qualitative (categorical) data describes attributes or categories rather than quantities.

quiz.q: First-hand, unprocessed information collected directly by an investigator for a specific purpose is called …… data.
quiz.why: Primary data is original and collected directly for the current research purpose, unlike secondary data which was collected earlier by someone else.

quiz.q: Data extracted from the published records of an existing institution is an example of:
quiz.why: Data taken from records already compiled by someone else, for another purpose, is secondary data.

quiz.q: Data drawn from an organisation's own reports and records, such as its profit-and-loss account, is data from a(n) …… source.
quiz.why: Internal sources are the organisation's own records; external sources come from outside the organisation.

quiz.q: Data obtained from outside the organisation, such as tourism figures sourced from another company, is data from a(n) …… source.
quiz.why: External sources originate outside the organisation using the data, as opposed to its own internal records.

quiz.q: Which data-collection method involves the investigator visiting the respondent in person?
quiz.why: The direct personal interview method specifically involves the investigator meeting the respondent face to face.

quiz.q: In the indirect oral interview method, the investigator obtains information by:
quiz.why: Indirect oral interviews question third parties who are in touch with the actual informants, rather than the informants themselves.

quiz.q: A key disadvantage of collecting data through correspondents is:
opts: Lack of conformity and unreliable data
quiz.why: Local correspondents collecting data on an investigator's behalf often produce data lacking uniformity and reliability.

quiz.q: Which data-collection method lacks visual feedback from the respondent?
quiz.why: A telephone interview is audio-only, so the interviewer cannot see the respondent's expressions or body language.

quiz.q: A major advantage of the mailed questionnaire method is that:
opts: It guarantees a high response rate
It requires no postage or distribution cost
quiz.why: With no interviewer present, mailed questionnaires preserve anonymity and remove interviewer bias, though response rates are typically low.

quiz.q: The observation method is best described as a method concerned with:
opts: Actual perception of behaviour rather than what respondents say
quiz.why: Observation records what people actually do, rather than relying on self-reported answers.

quiz.q: In the experimental method, the researcher:
opts: Holds other variables constant, manipulating one
quiz.why: The experimental method isolates the effect of one variable by holding the others constant while it is deliberately changed.

quiz.q: A good questionnaire is typically divided into which three parts?
opts: Introduction, personal data, and actual questions
quiz.why: A well-designed questionnaire opens with an introduction, gathers personal data, then presents the actual research questions.

quiz.q: All the following are qualities of a good questionnaire, EXCEPT:
quiz.why: Leading questions bias the respondent toward a particular answer and should be avoided, not used, in a well-designed questionnaire.

quiz.q: The process of selecting a required number of items or persons from a population is called:
quiz.why: Sampling is specifically the act of selecting a subset of a population for study.

quiz.q: The totality of items or measurements a researcher is interested in studying is called the:
quiz.why: The population (or universe) is the entire set the researcher wants to study; a sample is only a subset of it.

quiz.q: Sampling in which every unit of the population has a known, non-zero chance of selection is called …… sampling.
quiz.why: Probability sampling is defined by every unit having a known, non-zero chance of being selected.

quiz.q: Dividing a population into strata and drawing a simple random sample from each is called:
quiz.why: Stratified sampling divides the population into meaningful groups (strata) and samples randomly within each one.

quiz.q: Selecting the first unit at random and then choosing subsequent units at fixed, regular intervals is called:
quiz.why: Systematic sampling fixes a regular interval after a random starting point, unlike stratified or cluster sampling.

quiz.q: A sampling method where the population is divided into clusters and entire clusters are randomly selected is called:
quiz.why: Cluster sampling randomly selects whole clusters (such as geographic zones) rather than individuals within strata.
